lead: As an aircraft grows bigger and faster, the air load on a flap or elevator grows far faster than a pilot's arm. Hydraulics supplies the missing force. In a power-assisted system the mechanical link from Chapter 1.2 stays and a hydraulic boost acts in parallel with it. In a fully powered system the link is deleted and actuators alone move the surface. All large transports and most fighters are fully powered, while smaller types often stay power-assisted. This chapter shows why the force outgrows the pilot, how the boost loop closes, and what redundancy an irreversible system needs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for the mechanical link that the boost sits in parallel with.

sections.h3: Why the pilot's arm runs out

blocks.text: The air load is spread over the whole control surface. Each small element of load sits at some distance behind the hinge, and the sum of load times that distance is the hinge moment M, which the pilot's linkage must carry.
M = q S c C_h,   q = ½ ρ V²
blocks.where: M is the hinge moment in N·m; q is the dynamic pressure in Pa; ρ is air density in kg/m³; V is true airspeed in m/s; S is the surface area in m²; c is its chord (mean width) in m; and C_h is the dimensionless hinge moment coefficient, set by shape and deflection.

blocks.text: Two things make M grow fast. Speed enters as V², so doubling speed quadruples the moment. Size is worse: area S grows with the square of a length L and chord c grows with L, so M grows with L³. An aircraft twice as long needs about eight times the hinge moment at the same C_h and speed. A trainer at 60 m/s and an airliner at 250 m/s differ by (250/60)² ≈ 17 in q alone.

A pilot can hold roughly 150–200 N of steady stick force, and perhaps 350 N in a short sharp pull. With a stick arm near 0.3 m, that is only tens of newton-metres. Once M reaches a few hundred N·m, a pure rod-and-cable link cannot do the job. Hydraulics closes the gap.

A power-assisted system — also called boosted, servo-assisted or partial power — keeps the mechanical link and adds a hydraulic actuator in parallel with it. The pilot's command still travels down the rods or cables; the actuator only shares the load.

items: The pilot moves the column, and the input linkage shifts the spool of a servo valve.
The open valve meters hydraulic fluid at system pressure into one side of the actuator.
The piston drives the surface, and its force is summed with the pilot's own rod at a summing lever.
A follow-up linkage from the surface back to the valve returns the spool to neutral when the surface reaches the demanded angle, which stops the motion.
With the valve closed and the pilot's hand off the control, trapped fluid locks the actuator and the surface holds its position.

blocks.text: The follow-up linkage is position feedback. Without it the valve would stay open and the surface would run to its stop. The boost ratio is the total hinge moment divided by the share the pilot's linkage carries, so a ratio of 30 means the pilot supplies 1/30 of the moment and the hydraulics supply about 97%. Ratios of about 20 to 40 are common. Because part of the load still comes back up the linkage, the pilot keeps a natural feel of the air.

If the hydraulics fail, the pilot can still fly. This is manual reversion. A bypass valve, or an open-centre servo valve, lets fluid move freely between the two sides of the actuator, so the surface is no longer locked. The pilot's rods and cables then drive it directly, with much higher stick forces and a restricted speed. Several smaller transports, turboprops, trainers and business jets use boosted controls for exactly this reason.

A fully powered system — also called irreversible or all-powered — deletes the manual path. The pilot's input only positions a servo valve, or tells a flight control computer what is wanted. Actuators alone move the surface. All large transports and most fighters are built this way, while smaller types often stay power-assisted.

Irreversible means the surface cannot drive back. Fluid trapped by a closed servo valve locks the actuator, so an air load cannot push the piston and cannot move the pilot's control. That is good: a gust does not snatch the stick. It is also the catch: with the link gone, the pilot has no natural feel at all, and an artificial feel system becomes compulsory (see Chapter 1.4).

items: Redundancy: two or three actuators per surface, fed by separate hydraulic systems, so one system failure still leaves control.
Jamming: a seized actuator can hold a surface hard over. Separate actuators, jam detection and sometimes a breakable connection limit the damage.
Rate limiting: flow, not pressure, sets how fast the surface moves. At high q the surface may lag the command and the lag can feed a pilot-induced oscillation.
Dissimilarity: channels are deliberately not identical, for example hydraulic on one and electric on another, so one fault type cannot take all of them.

blocks.text: Power-actuated systems go further. An electro-hydrostatic actuator carries its own small pump, driven by an electric motor bolted at the surface, and draws only electrical power and a little fluid. This removes long runs of high-pressure pipe, which leak and are heavy, but the electrical generation must grow to match (see Unit 3, Aircraft Electrical Systems and Instruments).

figure.caption: The pilot's linkage opens the servo valve; the actuator adds hydraulic force in parallel, and the follow-up linkage recentres the valve once the surface reaches the commanded angle.

spec.title: Power-assisted loop
spec.aria: Pilot input opens a servo valve, hydraulic pressure drives the actuator, and a follow-up linkage returns the valve to neutral when the surface reaches the commanded position.

examples.question: An elevator has area S = 4 m², chord c = 0.5 m and hinge moment coefficient C_h = 0.15 at 100 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m³. (a) Find the hinge moment. (b) The pilot can give 200 N on a stick whose arm to the circuit is 0.30 m. Find the boost ratio needed. (c) Find the hinge moment at 200 m/s.
steps: Dynamic pressure: q = ½ ρ V² = 0.5 × 1.225 × 100² = 6125 Pa.
Hinge moment: M = q S c C_h = 6125 × 4 × 0.5 × 0.15 = 1837.5 N·m.
Boost ratio = M ÷ pilot moment = 1837.5 ÷ 60 ≈ 30.6 (total hinge moment ÷ the pilot's share), so the hydraulics supply about 97% of the moment.
examples.answer: The hinge moment is 1837.5 N·m, a boost ratio of about 30.6 is needed, and at 200 m/s the same surface needs 7350 N·m.

traps: Saying a fully powered aircraft needs no feel system. It is the exact opposite: with the link gone, artificial feel is the only thing giving the pilot any stick force.
Calling a boosted system irreversible. A power-assisted system keeps the mechanical link and can revert to manual, with heavy forces.
Using V instead of V² in q, or dropping the chord c. Treat c and C_h as separate factors; C_h is dimensionless, c is in metres.
Thinking the follow-up linkage adds feel. It is position feedback that closes the loop and stops the surface at the commanded angle.
Believing higher hydraulic pressure gives a faster surface. Pressure sets the force; flow sets the rate.

quiz.q: Define hinge moment and write its formula with the meaning of each symbol.
quiz.a: The moment of the air load about the surface hinge: M = q S c C_h, with q = ½ρV² dynamic pressure in Pa, S area in m², c chord in m, C_h the dimensionless hinge moment coefficient.

quiz.q: Why does the hinge moment grow with the cube of aircraft size?
quiz.a: Area grows with L² and chord with L, so the product S·c grows with L³. Doubling size multiplies M by about eight at the same C_h and speed.

quiz.q: A rudder has S = 2 m², c = 0.4 m, C_h = 0.12 at V = 80 m/s, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Find the hinge moment.
A pilot gives 150 N on a stick with a 0.25 m arm. What boost ratio is needed to balance 1500 N·m of hinge moment?
Why can a fully powered system not be back-driven, and what does that force the designer to add?
quiz.a: The closed servo valve traps fluid and locks the actuator, so surface load cannot move the piston or the pilot's control. With no natural feel reaching the pilot, an artificial feel system must be fitted.

quiz.q: Why is a jammed actuator more dangerous than a failed one, and how is the risk reduced?
quiz.a: A failed actuator simply stops helping; a jammed one can hold the surface hard over and defeat the other channels. Designers use separate actuators on separate systems, jam detection and sometimes a breakable connection so the surface can still be moved.

quiz.q: What is the job of the follow-up linkage in a boosted system?
quiz.a: It feeds surface position back to the servo valve and recentres the spool when the commanded angle is reached, so the surface stops instead of running to its limit.

beyond: Not for the exam. The trend is the more-electric aircraft: replace central hydraulics with local electro-hydrostatic actuators and electromechanical actuators, then let the flight control computers decide which actuator does what. That turns a hardware redundancy problem into a control allocation problem, where a faulty surface is compensated by the others. Research also looks at jam-tolerant actuators and health monitoring that predicts a failing pump before flight. Search terms: power-by-wire, electro-hydrostatic actuator, fault-tolerant control allocation, more-electric aircraft.
